The results show that our method is the fastest (in alignment with Figure 5), while still achieving comparable classification performance, with accuracy, precision, and recall all around 0.97 and standard deviations in the range of 0.02 to 0.05. In addition, LADMM attains a comparable proximal-gradient mapping residual. Among the newly included baselines, PLADMM performs similarly to LADMM in terms of accuracy, recall, precision, and ResPG, but has a slightly larger computational time. PALM also remains faster than ADMM and MM in this experiment, although its stationarity residual is larger. DCA attains slightly higher average classification metrics, but the differences are small relative to the reported standard deviations, and its average computational time is higher than that of LADMM. Taken together, these findings demonstrate that LADMM achieves competitive predictive quality and comparable stationarity residuals while delivering the lowest computational cost.

To further examine the computational behavior of the methods as the problem size increases, we perform a scaling study for LOG-regularized logistic regression (45). We set m=4​nm=4n and test n∈{50,100,200,300}n\in\{50,100,200,300\} and we fix ρ=1\rho=1, λ=0.0063\lambda=0.0063, and ϵ=0.01\epsilon=0.01. Table 4 reports the average computational time over ten random instances. The results show that LADMM remains among the fastest methods over the tested range. These results provide additional evidence of the computational efficiency of LADMM.

5 Conclusion

We studied an optimization problem involving the sum of two functions (1), where one function is convex and differentiable and the other is weakly convex (but not necessarily differentiable). This setting naturally captures a broader family of optimization models that go beyond the convex regime. Numerically, we applied both ADMM and its linearized variant to solve the problem, with the latter reducing the need for nested loops. Theoretically, we showed that both ADMM and LADMM iterates admit a subsequence converging to a directional stationary solution under mild conditions. Both convergence guarantees rely on explicit and verifiable conditions on the penalty parameter: ρ>max⁡{σg,2​Lip∇f}\rho>\max\{\sigma_{g},\sqrt{2}\mathrm{Lip}_{\nabla f}\} for ADMM (Theorem 3) and ρ>max⁡{σg,1+Lip∇f,Lip∇f​(1+2​Lip∇f)}\rho>\max\{\sigma_{g},1+\mathrm{Lip}_{\nabla f},\mathrm{Lip}_{\nabla f}(1+2\mathrm{Lip}_{\nabla f})\} for LADMM (Theorem 4). The stronger condition for LADMM reflects the additional control needed to absorb the lagged-gradient effect introduced by linearization. Numerical experiments on two low-dimensional smooth functions and a high-dimensional logistic regression problem demonstrate the practical efficiency of the proposed ADMM and LADMM algorithms compared with baseline methods. In the LOG-regularized logistic regression setting, LADMM achieved classification performance and proximal-gradient mapping residuals comparable to the competing baselines, while having the lowest average computational time. These results suggest that LADMM provides an efficient strategy for this weakly convex regularized logistic-regression model.

Some promising extensions include inexact updates that are attractive for large-scale learning problems, acceleration and preconditioning techniques within the weakly convex ADMM framework, and extending the convergence analysis to cover linearization of the weakly convex term (as employed in Sections 4.1 and 4.2).

Appendix A Three-Hump Camel Function

A.1 ADMM for Three-Hump Camel

By setting f⁡(𝐱)=2​x12+x22f(\mathbf{x})=2x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2} and g⁡(𝐱)=x166+x1​x2−1.05​x14g(\mathbf{x})=\frac{x_{1}^{6}}{6}+x_{1}x_{2}-1.05x_{1}^{4}, we express the Three-Hump Camel Function (40) into the general form of (1). It is straightforward that f⁡(𝐱)f(\mathbf{x}) is convex. Here we verify that g⁡(𝐱)g(\mathbf{x}) is weakly convex, which requires to finding a constant σ>0\sigma>0 such that g^​(𝐱)=g⁡(𝐱)+σ2​‖𝐱‖2\hat{g}(\mathbf{x})=g(\mathbf{x})+\frac{\sigma}{2}\|\mathbf{x}\|^{2} is convex. We compute the Hessian matrix of g^\hat{g}

∇2g^​(𝐱)=[5​x14−12.6​x12+σ11σ].\displaystyle\nabla^{2}\hat{g}(\mathbf{x})=\begin{bmatrix}5x_{1}^{4}-12.6x_{1}^{2}+\sigma&1\\ 1&\sigma\end{bmatrix}. (S1)

For any vector [a,b]T[a,b]^{T}, we have

[ab]​[5​x14−12.6​x12+σ11σ]​[ab]=(5​x14−12.6​x12+σ−1)​a2+(a+b)2+(σ−1)​b2.\displaystyle\begin{bmatrix}a&b\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5x_{1}^{4}-12.6x_{1}^{2}+\sigma&1\\ 1&\sigma\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}a\\ b\end{bmatrix}=(5x_{1}^{4}-12.6x_{1}^{2}+\sigma-1)a^{2}+(a+b)^{2}+(\sigma-1)b^{2}.

Completing the square for 5​x14−12.6​x12+σ−1=5​(x12−1.26)2+σ−8.9385x_{1}^{4}-12.6x_{1}^{2}+\sigma-1=5(x_{1}^{2}-1.26)^{2}+\sigma-8.938 shows that the expression is nonnegative for all x1x_{1}, provided σ≥8.938\sigma\geq 8.938. Therefore, g^​(𝐱)\hat{g}(\mathbf{x}) is convex, and hence g⁡(𝐱)g(\mathbf{x}) is weakly convex.

Next, we estimate the Lipschitz constant of the function f⁡(𝐱)=2​x12+x22.f(\mathbf{x})=2x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}. Since

∇f​(𝐱)=(4​x12​x2),∇2f​(𝐱)=(4002),\nabla f(\mathbf{x})=\begin{pmatrix}4x_{1}\\ 2x_{2}\end{pmatrix},\qquad\nabla^{2}f(\mathbf{x})=\begin{pmatrix}4&0\\ 0&2\end{pmatrix},

we have Lip∇f=‖∇2f‖2=4,\mathrm{Lip}_{\nabla f}=\|\nabla^{2}f\|_{2}=4, and hence a sufficient condition in Theorem 3 for the convergence guarantee is ρ>max⁡{σg,2​Lip∇f}=max⁡{8.938,4​2}=8.938.\rho>\max\{\sigma_{g},\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{Lip}_{\nabla f}\}=\max\{8.938,4\sqrt{2}\}=8.938. In the experiments, We set ρ=100\rho=100, which satisfies this condition.

For the special forms of f⁡(⋅)f(\cdot) and g⁡(⋅)g(\cdot), we elaborate on how to solve the 𝐱\mathbf{x}- and 𝐳\mathbf{z}-subproblems in the ADMM iteration (4). Specifically, the 𝐱\mathbf{x}-subproblem in (4) is equivalent to

𝐱t+1∈argmin𝐱g​(𝐱)+ρ2​‖𝐱−𝐳t+𝐯t‖22≜G1​(𝐱),\displaystyle\mathbf{x}^{t+1}\in\operatornamewithlimits{argmin}_{\mathbf{x}}g(\mathbf{x})+\frac{\rho}{2}\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{z}^{t}+\mathbf{v}^{t}\|_{2}^{2}\triangleq G_{1}(\mathbf{x}), (S2)

where G1​(𝐱)=x166+x1​x2−1.05​x14+ρ2​‖𝐱−𝐳t+𝐯t‖22.G_{1}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{x_{1}^{6}}{6}+x_{1}x_{2}-1.05x_{1}^{4}+\frac{\rho}{2}\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{z}^{t}+\mathbf{v}^{t}\|_{2}^{2}. Taking the gradient of G1​(𝐱)G_{1}(\mathbf{x}) with respect to 𝐱\mathbf{x}, we get

∇G1​(𝐱)=[x15+x2−4.2​x13x1]+ρ​[x1−z1t+v1tx2−z2t+v2t],\displaystyle\nabla G_{1}(\mathbf{x})=\begin{bmatrix}x_{1}^{5}+x_{2}-4.2x_{1}^{3}\\ x_{1}\\ \end{bmatrix}+\rho\begin{bmatrix}x_{1}-z_{1}^{t}+v_{1}^{t}\\ x_{2}-z_{2}^{t}+v_{2}^{t}\end{bmatrix},

and hence the gradient descent update is given by

𝐱k+1=𝐱k−τ1∇G1(𝐱k),\displaystyle\mathbf{x}_{k+1}=\mathbf{x}_{k}-\tau_{1}\nabla G_{1}(\mathbf{x}_{k}), (S3)

where τ1>0\tau_{1}>0 is a constant step size and the subscript kk denotes the inner iteration number, as opposed to superscript tt for outer iterations. We repeat the gradient descent iterations in (S3) until convergence is achieved, i.e., when ∇G1​(𝐱k)<10−2\nabla G_{1}(\mathbf{x}_{k})<10^{-2}. We then set 𝐱t+1\mathbf{x}^{t+1} as the final iterate of 𝐱k+1\mathbf{x}_{k+1}.

The 𝐳\mathbf{z}-subproblem in (4) is equivalent to

𝐳t+1∈argmin𝐳f​(𝐳)+ρ2​‖𝐱t+1−𝐳+𝐯t‖22≜H1​(𝐳),\displaystyle\mathbf{z}^{t+1}\in\operatornamewithlimits{argmin}_{\mathbf{z}}f(\mathbf{z})+\frac{\rho}{2}\|\mathbf{x}^{t+1}-\mathbf{z}+\mathbf{v}^{t}\|_{2}^{2}\triangleq H_{1}(\mathbf{z}), (S4)

where H1​(𝐳)=2​z12+z22+ρ2​‖𝐱t+1−𝐳+𝐯t‖22.H_{1}(\mathbf{z})=2z_{1}^{2}+z_{2}^{2}+\frac{\rho}{2}\|\mathbf{x}^{t+1}-\mathbf{z}+\mathbf{v}^{t}\|_{2}^{2}. By taking the gradient with respect to 𝐳\mathbf{z}, we obtain the optimality condition:

[4​z12​z2]+ρ​[z1−x1t+1−v1tz2−x2t+1−v2t]=[00],\displaystyle\begin{bmatrix}4z_{1}\\ 2z_{2}\\ \end{bmatrix}+\rho\begin{bmatrix}z_{1}-x_{1}^{t+1}-v_{1}^{t}\\ z_{2}-x_{2}^{t+1}-v_{2}^{t}\\ \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0\\ 0\end{bmatrix},

which implies a closed-form solution for 𝐳\mathbf{z} given by

𝐳t+1=[ρ⁡(x1t+1+v1t)ρ+4ρ⁡(x2t+1+v2t)ρ+2].\displaystyle\mathbf{z}^{t+1}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\rho(x_{1}^{t+1}+v_{1}^{t})}{\rho+4}\\ \frac{\rho(x_{2}^{t+1}+v_{2}^{t})}{\rho+2}\\ \end{bmatrix}. (S5)

Under the stopping conditions of a maximum number of iterations and a sufficiently small gradient norm, the pseudocode for solving the Three-Hump Camel Function via ADMM is summarized in Algorithm S1.

A.2 LADMM for Three-Hump Camel

We intend to linearize the 𝐱\mathbf{x}-subproblem in (S2) by a first-order approximation of g⁡(𝐱)g(\mathbf{x}) at 𝐱t\mathbf{x}^{t}:

g⁡(𝐱)≈g⁡(𝐱t)+⟨∇g​(𝐱t),𝐱−𝐱t⟩.g(\mathbf{x})\approx g(\mathbf{x}^{t})+\langle\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{t}),\,\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^{t}\rangle. (S6)

The resulting 𝐱\mathbf{x}-subproblem becomes

𝐱t+1∈argmin𝐱⟨∇g​(𝐱t),𝐱⟩+ρ2​‖𝐱−𝐳t+𝐯t‖22.\displaystyle\mathbf{x}^{t+1}\in\operatornamewithlimits{argmin}_{\mathbf{x}}\,\langle\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{t}),\,\mathbf{x}\rangle+\frac{\rho}{2}\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{z}^{t}+\mathbf{v}^{t}\|_{2}^{2}. (S7)

Taking the gradient with respect to 𝐱\mathbf{x} and setting it to zero yields the optimality condition

∇g​(𝐱t)+ρ⁡(𝐱t+1−𝐳t+𝐯t)=𝟎,\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{t})+\rho\big(\mathbf{x}^{t+1}-\mathbf{z}^{t}+\mathbf{v}^{t}\big)=\mathbf{0}, (S8)

where

∇g​(𝐱t)=[(x1t)5+x2t−4.2​(x1t)3x1t].\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{t})=\begin{bmatrix}(x_{1}^{t})^{5}+x_{2}^{t}-4.2(x_{1}^{t})^{3}\\[2.0pt] x_{1}^{t}\end{bmatrix}.

Solving (S8) gives the closed-form update

𝐱t+1=𝐳t−𝐯t−1ρ∇g(𝐱t)=[z1t−v1t−(x1t)5+x2t−4.2​(x1t)3ρz2t−v2t−x1tρ].\mathbf{x}^{t+1}=\mathbf{z}^{t}-\mathbf{v}^{t}-\frac{1}{\rho}\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{t})=\begin{bmatrix}z_{1}^{t}-v_{1}^{t}-\dfrac{(x_{1}^{t})^{5}+x_{2}^{t}-4.2(x_{1}^{t})^{3}}{\rho}\\[8.0pt] z_{2}^{t}-v_{2}^{t}-\dfrac{x_{1}^{t}}{\rho}\end{bmatrix}. (S9)

With the 𝐳\mathbf{z}-update being the same as ADMM, i.e., given by (S5), the overall procedure is summarized in Algorithm S2. Compared with Algorithm S1, no inner iteration is required.

Note that this approach (Algorithm S2) differs to the LADMM scheme introduced in Section 2.2, where the linearization is applied on the smooth term ff. Since the weakly convex function gg does not satisfy the Lipschitz-gradient assumption, the convergence analysis developed in Section 3.3 is not applicable here, and we leave this extension for future work.

Appendix B Six-Hump Camel Function

B.1 ADMM for Six-Hump Camel

By setting f⁡(𝐱)=4​x12+4​x24f(\mathbf{x})=4x_{1}^{2}+4x_{2}^{4} and g⁡(𝐱)=x163+x1​x2−2.1​x14−4​x22g(\mathbf{x})=\frac{x_{1}^{6}}{3}+x_{1}x_{2}-2.1x_{1}^{4}-4x_{2}^{2}, we express the Six-Hump Camel Function (41) in the form of (1). Clearly, f⁡(𝐱)f(\mathbf{x}) is convex. To verify the weak convexity of g⁡(𝐱)g(\mathbf{x}), it suffices to find a constant σ>0\sigma>0 such that the function g^​(𝐱)=g⁡(𝐱)+σ2​‖𝐱‖2\hat{g}(\mathbf{x})=g(\mathbf{x})+\frac{\sigma}{2}\|\mathbf{x}\|^{2} is convex. To this end, we compute the Hessian of g^\hat{g}, leading to

∇2g^​(𝐱)=[10​x14−25.2​x12+σ11−8+σ].\displaystyle\nabla^{2}\hat{g}(\mathbf{x})=\begin{bmatrix}10x_{1}^{4}-25.2x_{1}^{2}+\sigma&1\\ 1&-8+\sigma\end{bmatrix}. (S10)

For an arbitrary vector [a,b]𝖳[a,b]^{\mathsf{T}}, we evaluate the associated quadratic form:

[ab]​[10​x14−25.2​x12+σ11−8+σ]​[ab]\displaystyle\begin{bmatrix}a&b\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}10x_{1}^{4}-25.2x_{1}^{2}+\sigma&1\\ 1&-8+\sigma\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}a\\ b\end{bmatrix}
=\displaystyle= (10​x14−25.2​x12+σ−1)​a2+(a+b)2+(σ−9)​b2.\displaystyle(10x_{1}^{4}-25.2x_{1}^{2}+\sigma-1)a^{2}+(a+b)^{2}+(\sigma-9)b^{2}.

We complete the square for the term 10​x14−25.2​x12+σ−1=10​(x12−1.26)2+σ−15.87610x_{1}^{4}-25.2x_{1}^{2}+\sigma-1=10(x_{1}^{2}-1.26)^{2}+\sigma-15.876, which is nonnegative for all x1x_{1} provided that σ≥15.876\sigma\geq 15.876. Consequently, g^​(𝐱)\hat{g}(\mathbf{x}) is convex, and hence g⁡(𝐱)g(\mathbf{x}) is WC.

Given the specific forms of f⁡(⋅)f(\cdot) and g⁡(⋅)g(\cdot), we outline the solution of the 𝐱\mathbf{x}- and 𝐳\mathbf{z}-subproblems in the ADMM iteration (4). The 𝐱\mathbf{x}-subproblem in (4) is equivalent to

𝐱t+1∈argmin𝐱g​(𝐱)+ρ2​‖𝐱−𝐳t+𝐯t‖22≜G1​(𝐱).\displaystyle\mathbf{x}^{t+1}\in\operatornamewithlimits{argmin}_{\mathbf{x}}g(\mathbf{x})+\frac{\rho}{2}\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{z}^{t}+\mathbf{v}^{t}\|_{2}^{2}\triangleq G_{1}(\mathbf{x}). (S11)

We solve (S11) using gradient descent. Taking the gradient of G1​(𝐱)G_{1}(\mathbf{x}) with respect to 𝐱\mathbf{x}, we obtain

∇G1​(𝐱)=[2​x15+x2−8.4​x13x1−8​x2]+ρ​[x1−z1t+v1tx2−z2t+v2t].\displaystyle\nabla G_{1}(\mathbf{x})=\begin{bmatrix}2x_{1}^{5}+x_{2}-8.4x_{1}^{3}\\ x_{1}-8x_{2}\\ \end{bmatrix}+\rho\begin{bmatrix}x_{1}-z_{1}^{t}+v_{1}^{t}\\ x_{2}-z_{2}^{t}+v_{2}^{t}\end{bmatrix}. (S12)

Then, the iterative update rule becomes:

𝐱k+1=𝐱k−τ1∇G1(𝐱k),\displaystyle\mathbf{x}_{k+1}=\mathbf{x}_{k}-\tau_{1}\nabla G_{1}(\mathbf{x}_{k}), (S13)

where τ1>0\tau_{1}>0 denotes the step size and kk indexes the inner iteration. We perform the gradient descent iterations in (S13) until convergence, which is determined when the norm of the gradient satisfies ‖∇G1​(𝐱k)‖<10−2\|\nabla G_{1}(\mathbf{x}_{k})\|<10^{-2}. The final value of 𝐱k+1\mathbf{x}_{k+1} is then assigned to 𝐱t+1\mathbf{x}^{t+1}.

The 𝐳\mathbf{z}-subproblem in (4) is given by

𝐳t+1∈argmin𝐳f​(𝐳)+ρ2​‖𝐱t+1−𝐳+𝐯t‖22≜H1​(𝐳).\displaystyle\mathbf{z}^{t+1}\in\operatornamewithlimits{argmin}_{\mathbf{z}}f(\mathbf{z})+\frac{\rho}{2}\|\mathbf{x}^{t+1}-\mathbf{z}+\mathbf{v}^{t}\|_{2}^{2}\triangleq H_{1}(\mathbf{z}). (S14)

Differentiating H1​(𝐳)H_{1}(\mathbf{z}) with respect to 𝐳\mathbf{z} yields the optimality condition:

[8​z116​z23]+ρ​[z1−x1t+1−v1tz2−x2t+1−v2t]=[00],\displaystyle\begin{bmatrix}8z_{1}\\ 16z_{2}^{3}\\ \end{bmatrix}+\rho\begin{bmatrix}z_{1}-x_{1}^{t+1}-v_{1}^{t}\\ z_{2}-x_{2}^{t+1}-v_{2}^{t}\\ \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0\\ 0\end{bmatrix}, (S15)

from which we obtain the closed-form solution for z1=ρ⁡(x1t+1+v1t)ρ+8z_{1}=\frac{\rho(x_{1}^{t+1}+v_{1}^{t})}{\rho+8}. For z2z_{2}, we arrive at the following cubic equation:

𝐳t+1=[ρ⁡(x1t+1+v1t)ρ+8z2].\displaystyle\mathbf{z}^{t+1}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\rho(x_{1}^{t+1}+v_{1}^{t})}{\rho+8}\\ z_{2}\\ \end{bmatrix}. (S17)

We present the pseudo-code for solving the Six-Hump Camel Function using ADMM in Algorithm S3.

B.2 LADMM for Six-Hump Camel

As in Appendix A.2 for the Three-Hump case, the ADMM 𝐳\mathbf{z}-subproblem for the Six-Hump Camel function (41) admits a closed-form update (see Appendix B.1), whereas the 𝐱\mathbf{x}-subproblem requires an inner iterative routine. To reduce this cost, we again consider a problem-specific linearized ADMM variant that linearizes the 𝐱\mathbf{x}-subproblem while keeping the 𝐳\mathbf{z}-update unchanged. As with the Three-Hump case, we do not provide a convergence analysis here and leave it for future work.

Specifically, we linearize the 𝐱\mathbf{x}-subproblem by replacing g⁡(𝐱)g(\mathbf{x}) with its first-order approximation at 𝐱t\mathbf{x}^{t},

g⁡(𝐱)≈g⁡(𝐱t)+⟨∇g​(𝐱t),𝐱−𝐱t⟩,g(\mathbf{x})\approx g(\mathbf{x}^{t})+\langle\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{t}),\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^{t}\rangle,

while keeping the 𝐳\mathbf{z}-update the same as in (S17). Following the same derivation as in Appendix A.2, the resulting 𝐱\mathbf{x}-update is

𝐱t+1=𝐳t−𝐯t−1ρ∇g(𝐱t)=[z1t−v1t−2​(x1t)5+x2t−8.4​(x1t)3ρz2t−v2t−x1t−8​x2tρ].\mathbf{x}^{t+1}=\mathbf{z}^{t}-\mathbf{v}^{t}-\frac{1}{\rho}\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{t})=\begin{bmatrix}z_{1}^{t}-v_{1}^{t}-\dfrac{2(x_{1}^{t})^{5}+x_{2}^{t}-8.4(x_{1}^{t})^{3}}{\rho}\\[8.0pt] z_{2}^{t}-v_{2}^{t}-\dfrac{x_{1}^{t}-8x_{2}^{t}}{\rho}\end{bmatrix}. (S18)

Algorithm S4 outlines the LADMM procedure to solve the Six-Hump Camel Function.

Appendix C Logistic Regression with LOG Regularization

C.1 ADMM: Logistic regression with LOG

By setting f⁡(𝐱)=1m​∑i=1mlog⁡(1+exp⁡(−bi​(𝐚i⊤​𝐱)))f(\mathbf{x})=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\log\left(1+\exp{\left(-b_{i}(\mathbf{a}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{x})\right)}\right) and g⁡(𝐱)=λ​∑j=1nPlog​(xj,ϵ)g(\mathbf{x})=\lambda\sum_{j=1}^{n}P_{\rm{log}}(x_{j};\epsilon) with PlogP_{\rm{log}} defined in (44), we express the LOG-regularized model into the general form of (1) in order to apply for ADMM. We start by verifying that f⁡(𝐱)f(\mathbf{x}) is convex and g⁡(𝐱)g(\mathbf{x}) is weakly convex.

Define a scalar function h⁡(s)=log⁡(1+exp⁡(−s))h(s)=\log\left(1+\exp{(-s)}\right) and denote the sigmoid function by l⁡(s)=11+exp⁡(−s)l(s)=\frac{1}{1+\exp(-s)}. We compute the first/second derivatives of h⁡(s)h(s) as follows,

h′​(s)=−11+exp⁡(s)=−l⁡(−s)≤0​ and ​h′′​(s)=l⁡(s)​(1−l⁡(s))≥0.\displaystyle h^{\prime}(s)=-\frac{1}{1+\exp{(s)}}=-l(-s)\leq 0\text{ and }h^{\prime\prime}(s)=l(s)(1-l(s))\geq 0.

Since h′′​(s)≥0h^{\prime\prime}(s)\geq 0 for all s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R}, the function h⁡(s)h(s) is convex. Note that the function f⁡(𝐱)f(\mathbf{x}) is a finite average of functions of the form:

fi​(𝐱)=log⁡(1+exp⁡(−bi​(𝐚i⊤​𝐱)))=h⁡(bi​𝐚i⊤​𝐱).f_{i}(\mathbf{x})=\log\left(1+\exp{\left(-b_{i}(\mathbf{a}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{x})\right)}\right)=h(b_{i}\mathbf{a}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{x}).

Since h⁡(s)h(s) is convex and non-increasing, and bi​𝐚i⊤​𝐱b_{i}\mathbf{a}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{x} is an affine function in 𝐱\mathbf{x}, it follows from the composition rule of convex functions that each fi​(𝐱)=h⁡(bi​𝐚i⊤​𝐱)f_{i}(\mathbf{x})=h(b_{i}\mathbf{a}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{x}) is convex. Therefore, their average f⁡(𝐱)=1m​∑i=1mfi​(𝐱)f(\mathbf{x})=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}f_{i}(\mathbf{x}) is also convex.

Then we estimate the Liptschitz constant of f⁡(𝐱)f(\mathbf{x}). Since 0≤h′′​(s)=l⁡(s)​(1−l⁡(s))≤14,∀s∈ℝ0\leq h^{\prime\prime}(s)=l(s)(1-l(s))\leq\frac{1}{4},\forall s\in\mathbb{R} and the Hessian of ff satisfies

∇2f​(𝐱)=1m​∑i=1mh′′​(bi​𝐚i⊤​𝐱)​𝐚i​𝐚i⊤⪯14​m​A⊤​A,\nabla^{2}f(\mathbf{x})=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}h^{\prime\prime}(b_{i}\mathbf{a}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{x})\,\mathbf{a}_{i}\mathbf{a}_{i}^{\top}\preceq\frac{1}{4m}A^{\top}A,

Lip∇f≤‖A‖224​m.\mathrm{Lip}_{\nabla f}\leq\frac{\|A\|_{2}^{2}}{4m}. (S19)

Next, we verify that g⁡(𝐱)g(\mathbf{x}) is weakly convex. In particular, Ke et al. [2021, Lemma 2.1] implies that for any σ≥23​3​ϵ\sigma\geq\frac{2}{3\sqrt{3}\,\epsilon}, the function

P^log​(x,ϵ):=Plog​(x,ϵ)+σ2​x2\widehat{P}_{\log}(x;\epsilon):=P_{\rm{log}}(x;\epsilon)+\frac{\sigma}{2}x^{2}

is convex for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}. Therefore, Plog​(⋅,ϵ)P_{\log}(\cdot;\epsilon) is σ\sigma-weakly convex, and consequently gg is λ​σ\lambda\sigma-weakly convex on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. Together with the bound in (S19), we obtain a sufficient condition for Theorem 3, namely

ρ>max⁡{2​λ3​3​ϵ,2​‖A‖224​m}.\rho>\max\left\{\frac{2\lambda}{3\sqrt{3}\,\epsilon},\frac{\sqrt{2}\,\|A\|_{2}^{2}}{4m}\right\}.

𝐱∗=proxlog​(𝐳t−𝐯t,λρ),\displaystyle\mathbf{x}^{*}=\textbf{prox}_{\rm{log}}(\mathbf{z}^{t}-\mathbf{v}^{t},\frac{\lambda}{\rho}), (S23)

The 𝐳\mathbf{z}-subproblem in (4) is equivalent to

𝐳t+1∈argmin𝐳f​(𝐳)+ρ2​‖𝐱t+1−𝐳+𝐯t‖22≜H⁡(𝐳).\displaystyle\mathbf{z}^{t+1}\in\operatornamewithlimits{argmin}_{\mathbf{z}}f(\mathbf{z})+\frac{\rho}{2}\|\mathbf{x}^{t+1}-\mathbf{z}+\mathbf{v}^{t}\|_{2}^{2}\triangleq H(\mathbf{z}). (S24)

C.2 LADMM: Logistic regression with LOG

We now apply the LADMM scheme from Section 2.2 to the logistic regression with LOG regularization (45). Using the weak convexity modulus of gg and the Lipschitz constant of ∇f\nabla f derived in Appendix C.1, a sufficient condition in Theorem 4 becomes

ρ>max⁡{2​λ3​3​ϵ, 1+‖A‖224​m,‖A‖224​m​(1+‖A‖222​m)}.\rho>\max\left\{\frac{2\lambda}{3\sqrt{3}\,\epsilon},\;1+\frac{\|A\|_{2}^{2}}{4m},\;\frac{\|A\|_{2}^{2}}{4m}\left(1+\frac{\|A\|_{2}^{2}}{2m}\right)\right\}.

The 𝐱\mathbf{x}-update is identical to that in Appendix C.1 and is given by (S23). For the 𝐳\mathbf{z}-update, applying (7) yields the explicit step

𝐳t+1=𝐱t+1+𝐯t−1m​ρ​∑i=1ml⁡(𝐜i⊤​𝐳t)​𝐜i,\displaystyle\mathbf{z}^{t+1}=\mathbf{x}^{t+1}+\mathbf{v}^{t}-\frac{1}{m\rho}\sum_{i=1}^{m}l(\mathbf{c}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{z}^{t})\mathbf{c}_{i}, (S29)

where l⁡(s)=11+exp⁡(−s)l(s)=\frac{1}{1+\exp(-s)} denotes the sigmoid function, and 𝐜i⊤=−bi​𝐚i⊤\mathbf{c}_{i}^{\top}=-b_{i}\mathbf{a}_{i}^{\top}. The LADMM procedure for solving logistic regression with LOG is summarized in Algorithm S6.
